doc.title: Percy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Depression, the NRA and WPA ruin Father's business
summary: The National Recovery Act drove Percy Sr. out of business; the family went on WPA relief before he returned to work for a salary at the garage.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: We were really well off until the NRA, the National Recovery Act, during the Depression came, and it drove my father out of business. The little guy got squeezed out somehow under that recovery act. And it was a couple of years when my father had to be on WPA with Works Project [Progress] Administration, and he’d go stand around with a shovel to get a handout, more or less, and we were like welfare recipients. I had to go through the prejudiced, Irish neighborhood, with this little wagon to get this rhubarb and a bunch of horsemeat and canned meat and stuff. My father was really devastated.

And a couple years of that, and finally he went back to work at the garage on a salary using his tools and working on the same people that he had built up this trade. Anyhow, he got back up there on his working for somebody else, and he stayed at that garage through, well Bechtel sold the garage to a family of Wolfson’s. There were three generations of Wolfson’s that took over that business while my father worked up there. He was a loyal guy, he wouldn’t leave during the war to get a wartime job. Anyhow, that was Percy Sr., he was a loyal guy. We only saw him in the evening about an hour before we went to bed, or half hour before it was bedtime, for years and years while we were growing up.
